title: ALMA Pipeline Evolution
abstract:
The CASA/ALMA Pipeline is the standard data processing software for the Atacama Large (sub-)Millimeter Array (ALMA) radio interferometer. It has been developed by an international team over the course of more than 20 years and it is now used to process >95% of all ALMA datasets.

The planned ALMA Wideband Sensitivity Upgrade (WSU) will be enhancing the observing capabilities with larger bandwidths and better spectral resolution, leading to orders of magnitude higher data volumes which will need a new highly parallelized data processing system.

In this poster we describe ongoing work to prepare the pipeline for this future workflow based system. We discuss refactoring the interferometry imaging, the most time consuming step in the pipeline, to use faster characterization of features in datasets via region-of-interest detection, reducing pre-imaging workloads and mitigation strategies while limiting any scientific loss.

We are also working on analyzing the so called "Pipeline Context" which acts as a central hub to record stage results and to transport intermediate products for use in later stages. Its current mixture of use cases needs to be modularized and distributed to be scalable.

To enhance ALMA's "Fast Lane" delivery of pipeline results, this cycle we have worked on improving a number of our Quality Assessment (QA) Scores to allow for more robust identification of pipeline runs that can be immediately delivered to the PIs without detailed human inspection.

Finally, a large documentation restructuring effort using "readthedocs" has been undertaken to streamline and improve existing documents and facilitate adding more content which will help transfer the existing pipeline to the new data processing system.

track.name: Topical Computing, Software and Algorithms

title: Pythonic data reduction pipeline framework for ESO software stack
abstract:
In 2023, ESO approved the use of Python in instrument software packages, enabling developers to work at a higher level of abstraction than is possible with legacy C code. This can substantially improve code reuse and allow greater modularity through declarative and object-oriented programming.

Object-oriented design offers several notable advantages for pipeline development. Data items, their relationships and processing steps can be declared, reused, and extended with minimal effort. Human-readable descriptions of data items and algorithms remain closely integrated with the code, reducing the need to maintain separate documentation. Through use of introspection, automated testing for compliance with the specification can also be integrated into the development process, helping prevent inconsistencies. Most importantly, this approach enables us to decouple the general principles of data-reduction pipelines from the scientific objectives of individual instruments. Pipeline developers can therefore focus on instrument-specific requirements without the necessity to pay attention to the complexities of managing the data flow.

We present a generic Python framework for building data-processing pipelines, developed collaboratively by A* software group at the University of Vienna and Academia Sinica Institute of Astronomy and Astrophysics in Taipei, Taiwan. The framework is fully compatible with the existing ESO software stack (EDPS, pyesorex) while keeping dependencies to minimum in order to allow independent use. At the same time, it is already being employed to implement the data-reduction pipeline for METIS, one of the first-generation instruments of the Extremely Large Telescope, potentially paving the way for broader adoption across future instruments.

track.name: The art of collaboration in astronomy software development

title: VizieR versus increasing bot scraping
abstract:
The CDS VizieR service, like many Data Centers, is facing a dramatic increase in bot crawling. These are millions of queries each day, which pollute and impact the VizieR service. This massive and blind  harvesting targets static and dynamic resources and is generally controlled by AI to populate knowledge bases. Log analysis shows many queries, executed by a wide range of IPs, all of which look legitimate without any obvious AI marker: it becomes harder to detect their origin and to manage the flow.
Maintaining good availability for users requires redefining data access management. This is often done urgently, but in the background, the CDS is investigating access management for the long term. In this poster, we present the solutions used, the solution implemented today, and those planned.

track.name: Usability, accessibility and security in astronomy software

title: Astellum: A Morphological Feature Annotation Tool for Astronomy Outreach
abstract:
High-quality astrophotos are far more accessible to amateurs with the wide use of smart telescopes, cheaper equipment and social media sharing. Identifying what celestial objects are in the photos is well achieved by existing astronomy software. However, the process of recognising morphological features and generating audience-tailored explanations is still complicated. This step is essential in outreach, as it turns initial interest into sustained engagement with astronomy.

Astellum is an open-source outreach tool, featuring celestial object recognition, morphological feature annotation, and poster generation. A WCS-based feature atlas and AI-assisted explanation generation make it possible for audiences to understand professional astronomical images at a level suited to them.

Kiosk mode in Astellum is designed for public observing night events, through which users can understand the morphological features and the explanations in real time. Additionally, the other two modes, Atlas and Studio, provide advanced atlas management and outreach poster editing.

The tool is under active development and testing. We plan to evaluate it with school groups. ADASS will be a good opportunity to gather feedback from a wider audience.

track.name: Topical Computing, Software and Algorithms

title: Astronomical Projects with Multiple Repositories: A Portal for Consolidated Information and Kubernetes-Based Operations
abstract: # Astronomical Projects with Multiple Repositories: A Portal for Consolidated Information and Kubernetes-Based Operations **Authors:** E. Buchholz1, S. Borra1, M. Drobek1, L. Haupt1, H. Heßling1 **Affiliation:** 1 German Center for Astrophysics (DZA), Görlitz, Germany. **Date:** July 30, 2026 # Abstract The antennas and telescopes of the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO) will produce enormous data streams, making long-term storage of the raw telescope data impractical. Instead, projects such as ‘Transients and Pulsars with MeerKAT’ (TRAPUM) process the data streams in real time. They search for pulsars and transients, storing only data of scientific relevance. This real time processing is performed by a largely automated pipeline, though final steps still require manual inspection. The Machine-Learning based Pipeline for Pulsar Analysis (ML-PPA) project aims to eliminate the manual steps by providing a fully automated analysis pipeline for pulsar searches, developed by an interdisciplinary team of astronomers, physicists and data scientists. As the ML-PPA project continues to grow, the increasing involvement of researchers and the expansion of software have introduced challenges in maintaining a well-organised and scalable software structure. Such project needs to adopt modern engineering practices, including a Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipeline for each repository, test coverage and automated deployment of documentation. In addition to eliminating isolated information silos within the infrastructure, a single portal was set up to centralise all information. This presentation provides an overview of the software architecture of the ML-PPA project and explains how the portal and documentation for each of the sub-projects are automatically generated from the source code and made available online. In addition, containerisation and a Kubernetes infrastructure are used to operate the entire ML-PPA system. Both the repositories and the documentation remain in-house, which enables automated updates, thereby reducing maintenance costs in particular. Future additions to ML-PPA will follow this workflow to ensure high-quality, well-documented code that is seamlessly deployed on a modern infrastructure. The already substantial volume of software documentation makes it difficult to extract relevant information. Therefore, LLMs (Large Language Models) are to be integrated in future to facilitate the use of ML-PPA.

track.name: Building and operating science platforms and workflows in the Petabyte Era

title: Beyond XMMGPT: Agentic AI for Science Operations Centres, from Proposal Preparation to Catalogue Exploration
abstract:
Large Language Models are often presented as conversational interfaces, but their greater value for mission operations may lie in their ability to coordinate trusted tools, technical knowledge, and scientific services. 

XMMGPT is an Agentic AI prototype developed for the XMM-Newton Science Operations Centre that combines Retrieval-Augmented Generation over mission documentation with access to operational and scientific services through machine-readable interfaces.

Building on the XMMGPT prototype previously presented at ADASS, this contribution shifts the focus from an individual mission assistant to a reusable architectural pattern for Science Operations Centres. We demonstrate how an LLM can act as a mediator between astronomers and existing mission capabilities, selecting and invoking specialised services rather than attempting to reproduce their functionality. Current use cases include querying technical documentation, checking target visibility, exploring X-ray catalogues through natural-language-to-ADQL workflows, retrieving and generating scientific products, estimating pile-up and count-rate conversions, and accessing upper-limit and long-term light-curve services. These capabilities support an interactive proposal preparation workflow in which users can move from a scientific question to feasibility assessment and archive exploration through a single conversational interface.

The approach relies on constrained, well-tested, agent-ready services with explicit schemas, controlled parameters, provenance, and human oversight. This separation between a mission-independent AI orchestration layer and mission-specific knowledge and tools offers a practical route towards reuse across multiple missions and observatories, while retaining scientific traceability and operational control.

track.name: AI as a tool for data discovery and data management

title: A distributed system for collecting sky brightness data
abstract: The Dark Sky Protection Project aims to establish long-term monitoring of sky brightness at several sites of interest to NOIRLab. We present an open-source Python package for acquiring and managing data from SQM-LE and TESS-W4C devices, together with supporting components that enable their autonomous operation at geographically distributed locations. The system is designed for robust, unattended operation, with resilience to communication, hardware, and software failures. These capabilities provide a scalable infrastructure for long-term characterization of sky brightness and its evolution at astronomical sites.

track.name: Topical Computing, Software and Algorithms

title: ARCADIA: AI-based Real-time Analysis for Autonomous Space Systems
abstract:
The New Space Economy, enabled by the increasing availability of commercial launch vehicles and spacecraft, has renewed interest in lunar exploration. Within the Italian PRORIS program and the HARLOCK project, the Rare-earth & Heavy Elements Analyzer (RHEA) is being developed. RHEA is a payload consisting of a suite of instruments designed for integration on small rovers, enabling rare earth element (REE) and rare-metal scouting and prospecting through a highly coordinated and synergistic approach based on a progressive and multiscale observation strategy. RHEA combines gamma-ray spectroscopy, hyperspectral imaging, ultraviolet fluorescence screening, and X-ray fluorescence analysis to identify and characterize REE-bearing deposits and associated elemental and mineralogical signatures across different spatial scales. Its operation in the lunar environment is constrained by limited onboard power and communication bandwidth with Earth, making artificial intelligence (AI) a key enabling technology for autonomous scientific operations and onboard data processing.

We present the AI-based Real-time Computational Analysis platform for Decision Inference in Autonomous space systems (ARCADIA), which implements the Instrument Control Unit (ICU) and onboard Data Processing Unit (DPU) for the RHEA rover. The ICU controls and monitors the scientific payload, while the DPU performs AI-enhanced onboard data analysis, including spectral identification of REEs, real-time multi-instrument data fusion, and data reduction. These capabilities support the generation of scientific products, autonomous decision-making, and efficient use of communication bandwidth and onboard storage. Real-time onboard processing of scientific data enables ARCADIA to enhance the effectiveness of the scouting process by rapidly guiding the rover toward the most promising sites for further investigation, thereby accelerating target selection and exploration even during short-duration missions.

The ARCADIA software architecture includes interfaces with the rover and scientific payloads. A market survey of low-power Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) computing platforms was conducted to identify solutions meeting the project requirements for power consumption, computational capability, and environmental constraints. AI algorithms for onboard data analysis were evaluated on low-power edge-computing platforms, including the NVIDIA Jetson Nano, and on RISC-V processors representative of flight-proven hardware. Candidate platforms target a power consumption below 5 W while supporting AI models optimized through pruning and quantization, with the goal of enabling real-time onboard processing under lunar resource constraints.

The technologies and methodologies developed within ARCADIA are designed to be transferable to other autonomous space systems and adaptable to a broader range of future space missions.

track.name: AI as tool for scientific discovery

title: Sharing best practices for astronomical software, services and infrastructure.
abstract: The interoperability of astronomical software and services relies on the development and implementation of Virtual Observatory (VO) aware software. In practice this requires supporting structures that facilitate coordination and collaboration of the software developers and scientists who build these systems and contribute to the underlying infrastructure. While on-line platforms and forums have a role, we emphasise the importance of in-person events to break down barriers and provide an environment for effiicient exchanges of ideas and problem solving in hack-a-thon activities. We present the results of the Astronomy Open Science Competence Centre Pilot (Astro-CC Pilot) project, in particular the series of events that has enabled collaboration in the European astronomical community on the topic of implementing VO standards in tools and services. The Astro-CC Technology Forums, Data Provider Forum and Scientific Training events have reached a wide range of technical and scientific participants, and the results are helping us to define the requirements for a Competence Centre that would be integrated into an eventual Astronomy node of the European Open Science Cloud (EOSC).

track.name: The art of collaboration in astronomy software development

title: A New Method for Visualizing Multiband Astronomical Data in the Hue-Saturation-Value Colour Space
abstract: The visualization of astronomical data remains a key process in the modern astronomy workflow, providing the ability to generate diagnostics, identify features, and share results. By processing data in the HSV colour space, we expose the scientific and visual choices traditionally made implicitly in the RGB colour space. We present one such method of calculation in the HSV colour space for multiband images, for each of the three Hue-Saturation-Value channels. We represent relative spectral luminosity via the Hue channel, the spread of luminosity via the Saturation channel, and the combined luminosity via the Value channel. This method depicts noise, luminosity, and spectral differences so as to be able to better diagnose observation issues, identify and classify features, and depict multiband images when compared to traditional RGB methods.

track.name: Topical Computing, Software and Algorithms

title: AstroPhot: fitting everyhting everywhere all at once in astronomical images
abstract: Astrophot is a mature tool for parametric image modelling of astronomical images. One has the flexibility to construct arbitrarily complex models of arbitrarily many objects in a scene over arbitrarily many images at different epochs/wavelengths. This is done through an intuitive object oriented interface, and assisted by a large suite of detailed Jupyter notebook tutorials and documentation describing every model. It operates in PyTorch or JAX allowing for accelerated CPU or GPU processing; further, with a caskade backend it is able to trivially interface with other codes such as caustics to add gravitational lens modelling capabilities. In this talk I will detail some of the applications for which AstroPhot is already in use, as well as ongoing transient scene modelling work for the LSST.

track.name: Building and operating science platforms and workflows in the Petabyte Era

title: Prototyping a Space-Based Observatory Pipeline in Three Weeks with Claude Code
abstract: The TOLIMAN space telescope is a low-cost mission to detect exoplanets via astrometry, with a focus on the Alpha Centauri binary system, our nearest-neighbor star system. The data processing pipeline will be deployed on the Google Cloud Platform (GCP) to best cater to the international collaboration. The pipeline utilizes a persistent GCP Virtual Machine (VM) running the Dagster orchestration software. Each data processing task is packaged as a Docker image and executed as an ephemeral Cloud Run job, with processed data stored in a GCP bucket and a PostgreSQL database hosted on Google Cloud SQL.  The prototype, our first data pipeline on Google Cloud, was built by leveraging the Claude Code agentic coding tool, which facilitated rapid learning of the necessary tools. A streamlined development cycle enabled us to investigate, implement, and test in fast succession, resulting in a working pipeline within three weeks of initial conceptualization. We found Claude Code to be immensely useful but could result in unnecessary complexity and software bloat without proper human supervision. We will discuss our observations and recommendations for using Claude Code for scientific software engineering.

track.name: AI as tool for software engineering

title: A Unified Astronomy Thesaurus in the era of Large Language Models
abstract: The Unified Astronomy Thesaurus (UAT) is an open, interoperable community thesaurus that organizes astronomy concepts and their relationships. Its usage in the astronomical community continues to grow, alongside the expansion of its content to meet evolving community needs. This paper briefly outlines the rationale behind the UAT, describes its current curation process and release cycle, and discusses the challenges and opportunities it presents in the era of Large Language Models (LLMs).

track.name: AI as a tool for data discovery and data management

title: The NEOCC Observations Analysis Tool: Astrometric Residual Diagnostics and Unexplained Systematic Errors
abstract:
Astrometric residuals, the difference between the measured position of an object and the position predicted by orbital calculations at the time of observation, constitute a fundamental diagnostic as they can reveal limitations in the dynamical model or errors in the measurements. This can be particularly relevant for newly discovered asteroid imminent impactors which usually have only a few observation and astrometric errors could bias the orbital solution and the resulting impact prediction. Providing observatories with timely and transparent feedback on the quality of their astrometry is therefore essential for improving individual measurements and the overall reliability of the orbit solutions.

The ESA Near-Earth Object Coordination Centre (NEOCC) has recently released a new suite of free and publicly available tools for astrometric residual analysis, integrated into its NEO Portal. These include the “Observations Analysis” and “Observatories” pages[1, 2], together with a dedicated “Residuals” tab on individual object pages (e.g., (99942) Apophis) [3], offering interactive visualizations, advanced filtering, per-observatory statistics, and downloadable datasets[1]. Based on the output of the NEOCC orbit determination software Aegis[4], the tool shows astrometric residuals on demand for any object, at any epoch, and for every contributing observatory, transforming what was previously an internal diagnostic capability into a public resource.

We will demonstrate the tool live, showing how both professional and amateur observers can use it to assess the quality of their measurements, identify possible timing biases (e.g. Figure 1, left), and other systematic deviations in their astrometric submissions. It can be used to validate the overall performance of an observing system and to improve its hardware, software or configuration.

In addition to the live demonstration, we will present results from mining and analysing more than half a billion processed observations using these tools. We will present two still unrecognized systematic patterns in the mean astrometric residuals: one affecting the largest asteroid surveys (e.g. Figure 1, top right), and another one correlated with position on the celestial sphere (e.g. Figure 1 bottom right). The origin of these systematic effects remains under investigation, and a detailed analysis will be presented in a paper currently being prepared.

[1] https://neo.ssa.esa.int/observatories
[2] https://neo.ssa.esa.int/observations-analysis?tab=res_ra_vs_dec&obs_code=F51
[3] https://neo.ssa.esa.int/search-for-asteroids?sum=1&des=99942%20Apophis
[4] https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024CeMDA.136...58F

track.name: The art of collaboration in astronomy software development

title: Transitioning Subaru's Remote Observing Software to a Web Site
abstract:
A number of observatories use VNC (Virtual Network Computing) servers and
clients to monitor the observation screens from open-use observers
connecting from remote locations. Usually this involves a custom software
package that must be installed and configured with some sort of security key
and/or password to secure the system.  This puts an onus on software
developers to support multiple platforms (linux, mac os x and windows)
for the software, and additionally, provide support for installation issues,
connection issues and assorted remote troubleshooting.

We present a case study in transitioning from a remote software package to
a secure web site with second factor authentication at Subaru Telescope.
The site is supported by all modern browsers on all platforms, and provides
excellent viewing capabilities for all screens--without requiring any
intrusive changes on the observatory software side.  This transition has
allowed us to minimize installation hassles for remote observers and
greatly simplify troubleshooting and maintenance because there is no longer
any custom remote software for the user to install.  We discuss the
architecture of the new system, what pieces needed to be developed for the
observatory side and provide some limited anecdotal data on use (the system
went into use in August 2026).

track.name: Topical Computing, Software and Algorithms

title: Evolving the Data Central Archive: Scaling and Optimising Archival and Automated Data Reduction Systems
abstract:
Since the Data Central Archive began with the Anglo Australian Telescope (AAT) Archive in 2020, the archive has become an important service for Australian astronomy. It has since been expanded to include data from the ANU 2.3m telescope at Siding Spring Observatory and an automated reduction pipeline system for the instrument WiFeS. Reduced data for the 2.3m is also available and queryable through the archive.

However as the archive has grown in size to 1.3 million files for the AAT archive, query performance has declined. This poster will present how cone search query times were reduced by up to 95% using GeoJSON indexing in the MongoDB database backend. The poster will also present work on HiPS fibre table visualisations that have been generated from archival data for 2dF instruments on the AAT.

Finally, we will outline planned new additions to the archive: an automated data reduction pipeline for the Veloce instrument on the AAT, and an archive of a monitoring programme of Rubin Deep Drilling Fields using the Australian SKA Pathfinder (ASKAP). We will also describe ongoing work to modernise the backend to support direct API access, improving performance and scalability to facilitate the deployment of additional future archives.

track.name: Building and operating science platforms and workflows in the Petabyte Era

title: More Structure, Less Handwork: The New IVOA Document Repository
abstract:
The International Virtual Observatory Alliance (IVOA) develops standards that enable interoperability between astronomical data services and software. Maintaining these standards requires a reliable publication platform supporting document submission, metadata management, version tracking, and long-term accessibility.
The existing IVOA Document Repository combined a document upload interface with largely hand-maintained HTML pages. As the collection of IVOA standards and document versions across multiple publication stages and document types has grown, together with the need to accommodate additional resources such as errata and other associated digital artefacts, a more structured approach to repository management has become necessary.
We have developed a new system based on structured document metadata, initially populated from information extracted from the legacy repository. The system integrates with the existing ivoatex document preparation workflow and provides metadata validation and management, administrative review, and dynamic generation of document landing pages. The structured metadata model supports relationships between document versions, errata, supplementary resources, downloadable document packages, and associated resources such as XML schemas and bibliographic information from the NASA Astrophysics Data System (ADS).
In this contribution, we describe the current implementation of the new IVOA Document Repository, the design decisions adopted during its development, and ongoing extensions supporting the management and publication of IVOA standards documents and related digital artefacts.

track.name: Usability, accessibility and security in astronomy software

title: What does 10M€ EC-funding buy you? (e.g.) RADIOBLOCKS!
abstract:
The four-year, 10M€, RADIOBLOCKS proposal was submitted by a consortium of 33 partners on 15 April 2022 and already accepted  by 26 July. Work started 1 March 2023, which means the project formally ends 28 February 2027 - just a few months after this ADASS conference.

This timeline allows me to discuss the actual outputs realised by the project because all the work is realistically already finished by now.

RADIOBLOCKS aimed to improve key European radio-astronomical facilities (EVN, LOFAR, NOEMA, the Effelsberg-, Sardinia-, and Yebes radio telescopes, with a side-order of ALMA and SKA) along ALL the parts of the signal chain with the aim of improving field-of-view, sensitivity, and post-processing. A part of the project dealt with real hardware (actual receivers and hard-core semiconductor development), but with all signal chains moving from the analog to the digital domain asap, the project improves Digital Signal Processing across the board - in the widest possible meaning of the concept.

Of particular interest to this audience would be the (extremely) high throughput data transport (200-400 Gbps) straight into GPU memory, GPU-based processing (amongst many others replicating the unique science capabilities of the CPU-based VLBI correlator SFXC), but also touching on the aspect of graph-based algorithm execution (Dask), cloud-native data formats (MeasurementSet v4 based on xarrays w/ zarr backend) and the impact of that on processing, and, finally, bringing state-of-the-art Event Horizon Telescope-specific advanced Bayesian-inference based calibration and imaging algorithms (including _dynamic_ imaging!) to the centimeter-wavelength VLBI community.

My colleagues Mark Kettenis and Aard Keimpema have submitted abstracts about the results of (highly) specific tasks in the project, but in my talk I can put those into wider perspective.

track.name: Topical Computing, Software and Algorithms

title: xstar-tools: AI-Assisted Modernization of the XSTAR Photoionization Code
abstract:
Modernizing established astronomical software requires preserving scientific behavior while improving portability, maintainability, and integration with modern workflows. We present [xstar-tools](https://github.com/xstar-tools/xstar-tools), an open-source modernization of the FORTRAN XSTAR photoionization code through an AI-assisted software development. The project progressed from a pure Python implementation to an independent C++ engine with Python interfaces and native tools for generating XSPEC spectral tables.

Large language models assisted our code development, memory and runtime optimization, testing, and documentation under human supervision. Scientific qualification used FORTRAN XSTAR as the authoritative reference and examined atomic level populations, heating and cooling rates, convergence trajectories, radiative transfer, spectra, and output products. Validation combined numerical acceptance criteria with exact comparisons against accepted baselines. Qualification diagnostics exposed subtle differences in floating-point accumulation order, atomic level indexing, and the association of physical quantities with output records. Revised implementations were accepted only after passing the relevant qualification checks, with optimization changes additionally evaluated for memory use and runtime.

The xstar-tools suite also incorporates serial and local multiprocess execution, optional MPI execution for high-performance computing, and XSPEC table generation. Native packages are qualified on Linux, macOS, and Windows, with distribution through PyPI and conda-forge on supported platforms. These capabilities facilitate deployment and integration into other scientific applications while retaining the established XSTAR physical framework.

We discuss practical lessons from AI-assisted modernization, emphasizing the role of reference implementations, human evaluation, traceable diagnostics, and reproducible acceptance criteria in producing scientifically trustworthy software. Future development of xstar-tools will extend the framework toward post-processing hydrodynamic simulations.

track.name: AI as tool for software engineering

title: Activities at the SOFIA Data Center: Preserving a rich legacy of observations for the scientific community
abstract:
The Stratospheric Observatory for Infrared Astronomy (SOFIA) concluded flight operations in 2022, but preserving and expanding its scientific legacy also requires continued development of software, data products, and services. This part of the effort at the SOFIA Data Center (SDC), has evolved into a collaborative software engineering project that combines the expertise of astronomers, former SOFIA developers and newly onboarded engineers, ensuring continuity while introducing modern development practices and new capabilities.

A central aspect of this collaboration is the maintenance and evolution of the open-source SOFIA Redux data reduction framework. Managed through a Git-based development workflow, the project enables transparent collaboration on pipeline improvements, the integration of new processing features, and long-term software maintenance. Beyond the reduction software itself, the SDC has established reproducible mechanisms for publishing calibration reference files and derived data products through the DaRUS research data repository, providing persistent, citable access to the resources.

Collaborative development also extends to new software components that were not part of the original mission. We present progress on the SOFIA Imager Pipeline, which processes raw tracker camera images into science-ready products enriched with observatory metadata, including telescope pointing verified by plate-solve, observatory status information, and observing parameters such as chop beam geometry. These data products form an additional layer of information that supports scientific analysis and will be integrated into the public SOFIA archive.

To maximize interoperability, we publish our products through Virtual Observatory standards, enabling seamless discovery and use of SOFIA data alongside other astronomical archives. We further demonstrate new community services developed by the SDC, including the ATRAN_SDC web service, which replaces the discontinued NASA ATRAN interface and ensures continued access to atmospheric transmission calculations for infrared astronomy.

This contribution illustrates how collaborative team building, open software development, reproducible data publication, and community-oriented services together enable the long-term sustainability of a scientific data center. We discuss the organizational and technical practices that allow software and expertise from an operational observatory to evolve into a sustainable infrastructure supporting the astronomical community well beyond the lifetime of the original mission.

track.name: The art of collaboration in astronomy software development

title: Explainable XRF Element Detection with Embedding-Space KNN and Physics-Based Masks for the HARLOCK Lunar Rover
abstract:
In astrophysics, Deep neural networks have achieved state-of-the-art performance in a variety of spectral analysis tasks. However, these models are often considered "black boxes", providing limited insight into predictions and requiring post-hoc tools for explanations. This lack of transparency can limit their adoption in scientific contexts, as in these environments interpretability is essential. This is one of the challenges in the development of RHEA, the Rare-earth \& Heavy Elements Analyzer of the HARLOCK project within the PRORIS program. It combines gamma-ray spectroscopy, multispectral imaging, ultraviolet fluorescence screening and X-ray fluorescence analysis to identify Rare-Earth Elements (REE) deposits and associated elemental and mineralogical signatures across different spatial scales. 

In this work, we propose a model-agnostic framework that converts any Convolutional spectral classifier into an explainable predictor without hindering its performance on multiple metrics, demonstrating it on a complete model working with attention masks for additional insight and training stability. Our approach exploits the Neural Network's latent representation and preservation of spatial features: after training, the final regression layer of the backbone model is removed and replaced by a K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) regressor operating directly on the learned embedding space; as a result, every prediction is accompanied by an explanation in the form of the most similar spectra observed during training. This works particularly well thanks to a custom loss function designed to optimize the quality of the learned embedding space, without hindering performances. 

Furthermore, in our model, for each predicted element an associated attention mask is learned at training time starting from a physics-based initialization. This way, the framework provides, alongside instance-level explanations, easily readable heatmaps in the form of a mask-by-weights product, allowing users to trace model outputs back to representative examples in the training data and the relevant parts of the input used. Experimental results show that, in a regression task estimating the composition of soil samples, the average R2 score over the predicted elements stays around 0.9 for both the original approach and the explainable Deep kNN model (depending on the complexity of the task).

Our proposal offers a practical path toward trustworthy AI for spectroscopy, combining the representational power of deep learning with the transparency of example-based reasoning.

track.name: AI as tool for scientific discovery

title: AURIS.jl: A High Performance Radio Interferometry Software Suite
abstract: Most radio astronomy software was designed and developed over 30 years ago before parallel processing was the norm. Therefore, it does not take advantage of the high-performance computing resources that are available today such as new software technology in the form of on-the-fly compilation and advanced numerical algorithms like auto-differentiation. **AURIS** (***A**stronomical **U**tilities for **R**adio **I**nterferometry and **S**imulation*) is a Julia software suite designed to use the latest technologies whether that be now or in the future. This enables AURIS to process large volumes of data efficiently and accurately. All algorithms are designed to take advantage of the inherently parallel nature of radio interferometry data by distributing computations across multicore CPUs and GPUs, when available. In addition, AURIS by default uses half-precision (16-bit) floats for most calculations, which reduces the memory footprint and processing time by half without a decrease in accuracy. As a result, the AURIS calibration pipeline is over fifty times faster than the NRAO CASA calibration pipeline for VLA data, reducing calibration time from several hours to several minutes. This talk will discuss how the various features of the Julia programming language and its associated packages are used to implement a modular, high-performance software suite that can quickly and easily adapt to the increasing volume and wide variety of radio data, such as the *next-generation VLA* (ngVLA) and the *Event Horizon Telescope* (EHT).

track.name: Building and operating science platforms and workflows in the Petabyte Era

title: Disentangling AGN and stellar contributions to the Cosmic Spectral Energy Distribution using GAMA, SWAGX, EMU and eFEDS
abstract:
A galaxy's total radiation arises from a combination of processes including star formation, dust and gas reprocessing, accretion, and magnetic interactions. While star formation typically dominates the optical and infrared emission of galaxies, AGNs contribute significantly at X-ray, mid-infrared, and radio wavelengths. Even a modest AGN contribution can bias key derived quantities such as stellar
mass, star formation rate, and dust properties. To improve the accuracy of these measurements, it is essential to move beyond simple galaxy/AGN classifications and systematically disentangle their respective contributions. As a step toward this, we extend the GAMA catalog by incorporating new radio data from the SWAG-X survey and X-ray data from eROSITA for 5,258 sources within redshift z < 0.1 in the G09 region. We perform multiwavelength Spectral Energy Distribution (SED) fitting from ultraviolet to radio using ProSpect to derive stellar masses and star formation rates for these sources. For the first time, we present a Cosmic Spectral Energy Distribution (CSED) spanning X-ray to radio wavelengths, constructed by stacking the SEDs of individual galaxies, providing a more complete view of the integrated energy output of the nearby Universe.

track.name: Topical Computing, Software and Algorithms

title: Machine-Learning-Based Event Classification of Terrestrial Gamma-ray Flashes with a Segmented Scintillator Detector
abstract: Terrestrial Gamma-ray Flashes (TGFs) are sub-millisecond bursts of atmospheric gamma rays associated with thunderstorms and are of particular interest for space-based gamma-ray observations. Their detection from orbit requires the identification of brief gamma-ray signals in the presence of background, while operating under the limited computational and power resources typically available on CubeSat-class spacecraft. Within this context, the Gamma-Sky project is investigating low-power Edge-AI approaches for the real-time processing of high-energy radiation, using atmospheric X- and gamma-ray detector data. This work presents a machine-learning-based event-classification methodology for a CubeSat-class mission, exploiting the spatial and energy information provided by a segmented scintillator detector architecture. The proposed detector consists of multiple scintillator elements distributed throughout the detector volume rather than a single monolithic crystal. This configuration enables the identification of characteristic event patterns related to deposited energy, multiplicity of interactions, and spatial correlations between detector elements. The detector response is used to extract a compact set of event-level features suitable for machine-learning analysis. A dedicated algorithm is then developed to distinguish gamma-ray interactions from charged-particle-induced background, reducing the charged-particle contamination of a TGF event. The simulation results show that the spatial and energy-deposition information provided by the segmented detector offers effective discrimination between gamma-ray interactions and charged-particle-induced events. The processing chain is designed for resource-constrained onboard operation, with particular attention to reducing the computational and memory requirements of the trained models. Quantization and pruning are applied to obtain a lightweight implementation while preserving the event-classification capability. The resulting algorithm is suitable for deployment and experimental validation on embedded Edge-AI platforms. Preliminary results indicate the potential of combining detector segmentation, machine-learning-based event classification for background rejection, and efficient onboard processing in future compact high-energy space instruments dedicated to TGF observations.

track.name: AI as tool for scientific discovery

title: AI-Assisted PostgreSQL Engineering for NASA’s Near-Earth Object Surveyor Mission
abstract: The ground system for NASA's NEO Surveyor mission at Caltech/IPAC uses a heavily partitioned PostgreSQL database and Python tooling. This poster describes practical experience using large language models for code review, library migrations, schema and query design, and moving application database access to a stored-procedure API. The engineer defines the task, selects relevant context, and verifies each proposal. Controlled tests showed that AI can detect problems in application code but can also produce incorrect results when important context is missing. The poster presents a workflow in which AI drafts solutions, tests provide evidence, and the engineer decides what to implement.

track.name: AI as tool for software engineering

title: CANFAR Science Portal: Overcoming Challenges to Enable Next-Generation Astronomical Research
abstract: The CANFAR Science Portal has emerged as a cornerstone computational resource for Canadian astronomers and their international collaborators. Over the past several years, it has grown into a primary hub for astronomical research in Canada and beyond. Along with this growth have come challenges in providing a stable and performant system to a large and computationally demanding user base. I will discuss these challenges, the scalability and optimization solutions we implemented, and observed user patterns, such as peak usage trends and common workflows. As the CANFAR Science Portal (Skaha) prepares to become a major component of the SKA project, lessons from our pioneering system can guide its wider adoption by member nations. Attendees will gain insights into the technical and operational strategies that have enabled CANFAR to scale effectively, as well as actionable advice for deploying similar systems globally.

track.name: Building and operating science platforms and workflows in the Petabyte Era

title: The use of container in ASKAPsoft deployment
abstract: ASKAPsoft is a specialized software suite developed by CSIRO to process massive amounts of radio astronomy data collected by the Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP) telescope. It is currently deployed in Pawsey's HPC facility called Setonix. This poster explains the role of container technology throughout the process of ASKAPsoft development and deployment. Container hides a lot of complexities, but also creates some of its own. We would like to share our experience in navigating through these complexities.

track.name: Topical Computing, Software and Algorithms

title: Machine Learning Models for Predicting the COSI Background for Gamma-Ray Burst Detection
abstract: The Compton Spectrometer and Imager (COSI) is a NASA Small Explorer mission designed to study the MeV gamma-ray sky, including gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), compact objects, nuclear emission lines, and other high-energy sources. Reliable background prediction is important for transient searches because the background changes with spacecraft position, pointing direction, and time. The aim of this paper is to develop a probabilistic machine-learning framework for COSI background prediction to support GRB detection and localization. The framework consists of four main stages. The Angular Resolution Measure (ARM) method is used to filter the event data and generate light curves for different sky positions following the HEALPix grid. These background light curves are then used to train a probabilistic regression model and derive significance thresholds from its predictive distribution. The trained model is applied to the same sky positions within the COSI field of view to estimate the expected background. The observed light curves are then compared with the predicted background and significance thresholds to search for significant excesses associated with GRBs and support their detection and localization. In this work, we focus on developing and evaluating the background regression models using simulated DC4 background events and spacecraft information. For the regression analysis presented here, we use an ARM-selected background light curve with one-second bins. Spacecraft livetime information is used to select valid observing periods and remove bins close to South Atlantic Anomaly boundaries. The model inputs include the time elapsed since the start of the selected DC4 modeling interval, spacecraft altitude, the Earth-zenith direction, and spacecraft pointing orientation. The spacecraft pointing directions are originally given in Galactic coordinates and are represented in the models using Cartesian components. From the DC4 dataset, two consecutive orbits are reserved as a held-out temporal test block, while the remaining data are randomly divided into training and test sets. Only background events are used for model training and evaluation. We compare Poisson regression with a four-component Gaussian Mixture Regression (GMR) model, with the GMR providing a more flexible predictive distribution. The current results show that both models follow the large-scale evolution of the ARM-selected background. As future work, we plan to evaluate the trained background prediction models using simulated GRBs to measure their performance for transient detection and localization.

track.name: AI as tool for scientific discovery

title: Status of the IVOA Technical Standards and Processes as of 2026
abstract:
In recent years the Technical Coordination Group ([TCG](https://wiki.ivoa.net/twiki/bin/view/IVOA/IvoaTCG)) of the International Virtual Observatory Alliance ([IVOA](https://ivoa.net)) has continued the activities in developing community open standards targeted at establishing an interoperable scenario in the general astrophysical research domain.
Alongside the continuous work of revising or defining standards, activity has focused on requirements from research sub-domains that are re-emerging or have previously received less attention (such as time-domain astronomy or high-energy astrophysics), on technical challenges arising from new information system technologies (like OpenAPI), and on new data formats and distribution paradigms (including increased use of tessellation and distributed solutions). The [TCG](https://wiki.ivoa.net/twiki/bin/view/IVOA/IvoaTCG) has also discussed organisational aspects, possible improvements, and challenges of the [IVOA](https://ivoa.net/) standardisation process itself.
This contribution provides a brief overview of all of the above and tries to identify the major priorities that the [TCG](https://wiki.ivoa.net/twiki/bin/view/IVOA/IvoaTCG) might have to face in the oncoming years, balancing the available efforts volunteered by member projects and participating projects against the requirements for new or renewed standards and their uptake.

track.name: The art of collaboration in astronomy software development

title: Visual anomaly detection at scale using ThumP!
abstract:
The now operational Rubin LSST monitors the southern night sky and is forecast to send 10 million alerts (objects with significant changes in brightness) per night to brokers such as Fink. Fink is tasked with processing and filtering the alert-stream to manageable amounts for the individual researcher. During the first period of public Rubin alerts (February 2026), over 800 thousand alerts were streamed through the pipeline. Discovering anomalies and assessing image quality at scale in the real-time data streams of the Fink ecosystem is challenging.

ThumP! (Thumbnails? Prescreen!) was planned, implemented, and deployed successfully to visualize the first public alerts streaming through Fink providing confidence in the nominal operation and performance of the system. In the process ThumP! aided the discovery of 50 new supernova candidates and helped evaluate stream filters for good detections. This was achieved through ThumP!’s fast, dynamic visualization of Rubin thumbnails allowing the simultaneous (multi-user), parallel inspection and comparison of a large number (30 per minute) of candidate images. Individual visualizations can be adjusted interactively for easier comparison, annotated for quality control, and exported for further inspection or triggering follow-up with other telescopes. During the first public alerts stream ThumP! was deployed on a large-format tiled display wall, allowing  the local Fink team to inspect 12 000 alerts in a couple of hours.

ThumP! is open source and publicly accessible on the web.

track.name: Topical Computing, Software and Algorithms

title: MANNA: an MCP Architecture for NOIRLab, NRAO, and additional Archives
abstract: Astronomical data archives are an invaluable resource for research in modern astronomy. While many archives implement the same set of standards defined by the International Virtual Observatory Alliance (IVOA), differences in underlying data and architectural implementations necessitate significant archive-specific knowledge. This requirement can impede research, especially in multiwavelength astronomy. AI agents offer a promising way to lower this barrier, but without structured access to archive services and metadata they must rely on general knowledge or web searches, which are often incomplete or outdated for a given archive, and the searching itself costs time and tokens. To address this problem, we developed MANNA (MCP Architecture for NOIRLab, NRAO, and additional Archives), a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server tailored to IVOA-based astronomical archives that provides tools for archive discovery and data querying.  We found that MANNA improved performance across an evaluation suite of one open-weight and three Anthropic Claude models, increasing efficiency for all models and substantially improving accuracy for the smallest Claude model. This effect was magnified when limits on turns and time per task were applied to evaluated tasks, supporting the practical use of MANNA under budgetary or time-related pressure. Although MANNA was developed  mainly for the NOIRLab and NRAO archives, it is a flexible framework that is extensible to any IVOA-based archive.

track.name: AI as a tool for data discovery and data management

title: Exploring Roman Space Telescope Data in the Cloud: Integrating ipyaladin and Jdaviz in the Roman Research Nexus
abstract:
The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, launched on August 30, 2026, will return a data volume far exceeding that of Hubble and JWST combined, including wide-field images, spectroscopic data, and derived catalogs. The Mikulski Archive for Space Telescopes (MAST) serves this data via Amazon Web Services, and provides the [Roman Research Nexus](https://roman-docs.stsci.edu/data-handbook/roman-research-nexus) (RRN), a cloud-based science platform based in AWS, to facilitate exploration and analysis near the data.

This poster will focus on the integration of two community visualization tools, [`ipyaladin`](https://github.com/cds-astro/ipyaladin) and [`Jdaviz`](https://jdaviz.readthedocs.io/en/stable/), within the RRN's JupyterLab environment, letting astronomers explore Roman images, spectra, and catalogs side by side. Using sidecar and custom widgets, a flexible layout allows both tools to stay visible alongside notebook code, with the ability to synchronize viewport coverage, as well as source catalog and observation footprint display and selection. In the `ipyaladin` viewer, users can browse Roman imaging through [Hierarchical Progressive Surveys (HiPS)](https://aladin.cds.unistra.fr/hips/) and search data holdings directly from the displayed sky position.

We also describe our pipeline for generating these HiPS surveys from Roman image data using `astropy`'s `reproject` package at scale on AWS, touching on the cloud storage architecture, generation cost, and technical challenges of producing HiPS products at Roman's data volume.

Together, these capabilities give Roman researchers an integrated, cloud-native environment for visually exploring and analyzing imaging and spectroscopic data side by side, without needing to move data off the platform.

track.name: Building and operating science platforms and workflows in the Petabyte Era

title: Image-to-Catalogue: End-to-End Source Finding with a 3D large vision model
abstract: The next generation of radio astronomy telescopes, including the Square Kilometre Array (SKA), will generate unprecedented data volumes, requiring highly automated and reliable approaches for source finding and catalogue construction. Existing neutral hydrogen (HI) source-finding methods, including numerical algorithms and machine-learning approaches, have demonstrated strong performance but often rely on survey-specific preprocessing, parameter tuning, or architectures that do not fully exploit the three-dimensional structure of spectral-line data. We present the HI Segment Anything Model (HISAM), an automated image-to-catalogue pipeline for HI source finding based on a pretrained three-dimensional large vision model. HISAM adapts a volumetric segmentation architecture to HI spectral-line cubes through domain-specific modifications and fine-tuning, and integrates source segmentation with catalogue construction and false-positive rejection to transform input image cubes into science-ready source catalogues. We evaluate HISAM on the SKA Science Data Challenge 2 simulation. HISAM achieves competitive completeness and reliability for sources with sufficiently strong signals, while its overall completeness decreases when evaluated across the full source population.

track.name: AI as tool for scientific discovery

title: XPhotonBank: Enabling Scientific Discoveries through Photon-Level Management of Einstein Probe X-ray Data
abstract: The Einstein Probe (EP) is an interdisciplinary mission dedicated to time-domain and X-ray astronomy. Equipped with a wide-field lobster-eye X-ray focusing imager, the mission is capable of detecting up to 50 million photon events per day. Currently, the EP data processing pipeline adopts the observation ID as its basic data processing unit, it first rasterizes photon events into images, followed by source detection and the extraction of light curves and spectra. However, the use of a fixed exposure time in this workflow leads to two key limitations: it results in the omission of short-time-scale transients and faint sources, while also making it challenging to study the long-term evolutionary processes of celestial sources. To address these limitations and facilitate more flexible and efficient data analysis, we leveraged time-series database technology to develop XPhotonBank—a specialized database that organizes EP observation data at the photon-level granularity. Based on this database, we further developed a suite of data processing tools capable of generating customized scientific products (including images, light curves, and spectra) with user-defined time scales. Leveraging this framework, we implemented two complementary analysis approaches, data stacking and density-based clustering, which led to the discovery of a series of faint sources and short-duration burst events that were undetected in individual observations. These results demonstrate the potential of photon-level data organization to significantly enhance the scientific capabilities of the Einstein Probe or other high energy mission like eROSITA.

track.name: Topical Computing, Software and Algorithms

title: Meerkat: An Operational Software System for Automated Imminent Impactor Detection and Community Alerting
abstract:
The increasing discovery rate of near-Earth objects requires software systems capable not only of orbit analysis, but also of continuous data ingestion, automated decision-making, and rapid dissemination of actionable information. We present Meerkat Asteroid Guard [1], the European Space Agency's operational imminent impactor monitoring system, developed and maintained at the Near-Earth Object Coordination Centre (NEOCC). Since becoming operational in 2021, Meerkat has contributed to the identification and follow-up of all known pre-impact asteroid discoveries detected during its operational lifetime.

Meerkat continuously monitors newly reported objects on the Minor Planet Center's Near-Earth Object Confirmation Page, automatically detecting updates, retrieving observations, and executing orbit determination and impact assessment workflows. The system produces a range of data products, including impact probabilities, uncertainty visualizations, follow-up pointing recommendations, impact corridors, and object classification summaries, which are distributed to analysts and observers in near real time.

This contribution focuses on the software architecture and operational design of the system rather than on the underlying orbital algorithms. Meerkat employs a deliberately simple and maintainable architecture based on containerized services, automated pipelines, multiprocessing, and CI/CD practices. The software is designed for robustness, transparency, and ease of maintenance, allowing reliable 24/7 operation while remaining adaptable to evolving planetary-defence requirements.

Particular attention is given to the alerting framework. Through email notifications, messaging systems, and automated phone calls, Meerkat acts as a catalyst for rapid international follow-up campaigns. Through dedicated mailing lists, alerts are distributed to professional and amateur astronomers across multiple continents, enabling rapid follow-up observations to refine orbit solutions and confirm or rule out potential impact scenarios. Meerkat therefore provides a practical example of how astronomy software can bridge automated data processing and global scientific collaboration in a time-critical operational environment.

[1] https://doi.org/10.1007/s40295-025-00560-0

track.name: Topical Computing, Software and Algorithms

title: The SRCNet Federated Execution Framework: Bringing Scientific Workflows to the Data
abstract:
The SKA Regional Centre Network (SRCNet) will support scientific analysis through a federation of independently operated computing and storage facilities. Executing workflows across this infrastructure requires a common interface that accounts for data location, heterogeneous resources, and local scheduling policies.

We present the SRCNet Federated Execution Framework, a prototype that connects scientific workflow submission to execution on participating sites. A Computing Broker identifies eligible sites using resource capabilities and data locality.

Site-level Job Gateways provision pilot workers through local Kubernetes or Slurm infrastructure. HTCondor then matches queued workflow tasks to compatible pilots once resources become available, a mechanism known as late binding. This decouples task submission from worker allocation while allowing each site to retain control over its resources and scheduling policies.

The poster explains the architecture and follows a workflow from submission through site eligibility checks, pilot provisioning, execution, and status reporting. We illustrate the approach with the ICAL/Rapthor radio-interferometric calibration and imaging workflow, drawing on the prototype’s multi-node execution demonstration. We also discuss integration challenges involving authentication, delegated credentials, data access, and the boundary between federated services and site operations.

We conclude with lessons from building the prototype and priorities for operational deployment, including broader site validation, robust data staging, and execution identity management. The framework offers a concrete example of how existing scheduling technologies can support a common scientific execution service across heterogeneous astronomical computing facilities.

track.name: Building and operating science platforms and workflows in the Petabyte Era

title: Use of the AI for SRCNet development
abstract: The SKA Regional Centre Network (SRCNet) is entering its Science Verification phase, a period defined by tight milestones and a growing surface of interdependent services — registration, ingestion, metadata, and data access components among them — that must mature quickly without compromising long-term maintainability. This contribution reports on the use of AI coding assistants across SRCNet software development teams to meet these constraints. Rather than treating AI-generated code as a shortcut, our approach centers on structured prompting: requests are framed to explicitly encode target architecture and design patterns, module boundaries, documentation standards, and test coverage from the outset, so that output is usable beyond a first draft. In practice, AI-assisted code plays its strongest role in initial prototyping — standing up service skeletons, exploring API contracts, and validating design choices quickly — after which ownership passes to the responsible team for integration, hardening, and long-term maintenance. This handoff surfaces a recurring tension: AI tools can produce substantial, working code far faster than a team can meaningfully review it, and oversized reviews risk becoming a bottleneck or a rubber stamp, undermining the quality controls the Science Verification milestones depend on. We discuss practices adopted to mitigate this — smaller, prompt-scoped increments, review checklists aligned to architectural intent, and tests generated alongside code rather than after it — while showing that, managed this way, overall development velocity across SRCNet components can increase substantially. We conclude with early observations on where this approach has been most effective and where human architectural judgment remains indispensable.

track.name: AI as tool for software engineering

title: Bring Your Own Model: Treating AI as a Replaceable Part of the Science Platform
abstract:
Two options exist today, and each falls short in a different direction. Point a commercial AI application at data held on a science platform and the science turns into plumbing: credentials, staging, transfers, all for a dataset that should never have moved. Run a coding CLI inside the platform instead and it sits beside the data but sees only a shell and a filesystem — nothing of the archive, the session lifecycle, or the access rules governing them. The first cannot reach the data; the second cannot see the platform. Neither was built for research.
The scientific workbenches now appearing run on the researcher's own machine or cluster so the data need not move. But their domain readiness is built for the life sciences, and the integration path is proprietary: the platform arrives as a plug-in inside the vendor's application, and research context accumulates in that vendor's formats. Astronomy already has platforms tuned over decades to its data models, access rules and standards; we should not have to migrate onto a general-purpose workbench to benefit from these models — the models should meet our platforms on our terms.
I illustrate this with a client over CANFAR, Skaha and the CADC archives whose agent tools are not a parallel API: each performs the same action as a control in the interface, so astronomers and agents share one surface. Both launch, monitor and stop interactive and headless sessions, and the agent can task one with a script in an image carrying the astronomy libraries. Retrieved observations collected in a research area, products land in VOSpace, FITS and cube viewers give a fast visual read the model can be asked to assess, and workflows serve as written protocols the agent follows.
As this work is ongoing, the exact final vision for the user-facing product is still actively taking shape. Rather than presenting a finished system, we present our integration across CANFAR, Skaha, and CADC as the foundation and core of a future AI-enabled science platform. We bring these developments to ADASS to open a dialogue with the community—seeking to learn how researchers envision the natural blend of AI models and research workflows, and how our shared platforms can best deliver that vision.

track.name: AI as a tool for data discovery and data management

title: Machine Learning Methods for Imaging with Interferometers
abstract: We are on the cusp of astronomical analysis becoming data-swamped, with several next-generation instruments (SKA, Next Generation Very Large Array (ngVLA), Next Generation Event Horizon Telescope (ngEHT), etc.) related to radio-interferometry that are either in their final stages of planning or already under commission. The current method for cleaning dirty radio images is slow and difficult to automate, making it extremely challenging to handle large quantities of data. This will create a bottleneck in the data pipeline when the next-generation interferometers are finished being built. In order to not limit the discoveries that will come from these next-generation instruments, a more efficient method for processing data needs to be created. In this project, we use synthetic radio interferometry data to train a machine learning algorithm capable of deconvolving (‘cleaning’) dirty radio images.  The goal of this project is to develop an automated framework that is faster and more accurate compared to current image cleaning techniques.

track.name: Building and operating science platforms and workflows in the Petabyte Era

title: Pervasive AI as A Second Enclosure Movement
abstract:
What is the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) and the scientific and scholarly enterprise? I offer an answer to this question that draws on the history and scholarship of *the commons*. Historically, commons were shared agricultural land, most famously in preindustrial England. The term “commoner” simply refers to a person whose way of life depended upon the commons. In this sense, commoners and the historical English commons no longer exist, but not because of the well-known “tragedy of the commons.” Rather, the *enclosure movement* systematically converted them into private property of the wealthy and in so doing destroyed the commoners' way of life.

There are still commons today, but the most important ones consist of information, not farmland. They are cultural treasures like open-source software, Wikipedia, and the scholarly literature. From this perspective, scientists and academics are the new commoners, engaging in a distinctive “peer production” process that sustains the information commons. Although the tightening of intellectual property (IP) laws in the twentieth century has been referred to as a “second enclosure movement,” I argue that the rise of pervasive AI — ingesting essentially all existing information commons as input, and flooding them with new outputs — better deserves this moniker. In particular, generative AI interacts with peer production in such a way as to threaten the commons in a way that IP restrictions do not. It requires no extrapolations of the capabilities of AI systems to sketch a future in which the AI industry effectively appropriates the public wealth of the commons for private gain, in the process effectively destroying the commons and the way of life of those who depend upon them.

track.name: AI as tool for scientific discovery

title: Astronomy and Computing: strengthening the link between astronomy, software and computation
abstract:
Astronomy and Computing (ASCOM) was established in 2013 as a dedicated peer-reviewed venue for computational methods, software, data and infrastructure in astronomy. Born from discussions within the ADASS community, the journal continues to provide a home for research outputs that do not always fit naturally within traditional astronomy journals, while its scope has evolved alongside the rapidly changing landscape of astronomical computing.

In this poster, we present the current status and recent evolution of ASCOM. The journal has continued to grow in visibility and impact, reaching a 2025 Journal Impact Factor of 2.6 and returning to the second quartile of journals in Astronomy & Astrophysics. ASCOM received more than 1,700 citations in 2025, with its work cited extensively by the major astronomy journals, reflecting the increasing integration of computational methods and software into mainstream astronomical research. Its international community also continues to broaden, with authors from more than 60 countries and regions contributing over the most recent three-year period.

We highlight recent developments in the journal's scientific scope, publication model and Special Issues, and discuss how ASCOM is responding to emerging priorities including artificial intelligence and machine learning, large-scale computing and data processing, and sustainable scientific software and documentation. We also examine opportunities to further strengthen the connection between publication, software and reproducible research.

As ASCOM originated within ADASS, feedback from this community remains central to its evolution. The poster will provide an opportunity to discuss how the journal can best support astronomers, research software engineers and computing specialists, and how its scope should evolve to meet the needs of increasingly data- and software-intensive astronomy.

track.name: Topical Computing, Software and Algorithms

title: XMM-NEWTON SCIENCE ARCHIVE: Forthcoming Release of the New Angular-Based Portal
abstract:
The Science Archives, managed by the ESAC Science Data Centre (ESDC), continue to act as the primary repositories for ESA mission data, preserving scientific knowledge and ensuring accessibility for the research community worldwide. A key highlight in 2026 will be the launch of the new XMM-Newton Science Archive (XSA). Created in collaboration with mission experts, the new XSA introduces a next-generation approach based on  scientific use cases and workflows. The launch is planned for December 2026.
 
The modern interface will offer seamless exploration of X-ray sources with dedicated sections for exploring the available mission data, the XMM catalogs, the high level science products, and the image gallery. Built with the Angular framework, the archive benefits from a robust and maintainable architecture, a modular approach, enhanced performance, reusable components and a responsive user interface, which will provide a major improvement in the user experience. The new XSA follows concepts and reusable widgets now adopted across other ESA Science Archives, while also benefiting from shared components developed in parallel by other teams.
 
This release reflects ESA’s ongoing commitment to innovation, software excellence, and global collaboration in enabling access to and exploration of astronomical data.

track.name: The art of collaboration in astronomy software development

title: Pulsar Signal Segmentation and Analysis using Custom Convolutional Filter Stacks
abstract:
We present an ongoing investigation of a non-learnable approach for pulsar-signal detection using handcrafted 2D line filters. The method applies Gaussian ridge filters across multiple scales and orientations to identify the characteristic dispersed structures of pulsars in dynamic spectra. Small random perturbations are introduced into the filters, creating a noise-augmented filter bank whose responses are subsequently aggregated to reinforce consistent signal structures while suppressing uncorrelated fluctuations. 
The filter responses are processed through a sequence of sigmoid activation, nonlinear transformation, multi-scale summation, binarization, orientation alignment, and peak-prominence selection. This adaptive processing identifies orientations that provide consistent evidence for a pulsar signal without relying on learned convolutional kernels.
The current results on the B0531+21 dataset demonstrate the potential of this handcrafted filtering approach, with an overall F1-score above 90%.

track.name: AI as tool for scientific discovery

title: BIAS (Bias Images As Syntax): An AI Co-designed Esolang with Python and TypeScript Interpreters
abstract:
BIAS (Bias Images As Syntax) is a programming language that encodes logic as CCD bias frames. Inspired by Piet, it was created as an exercise in experimental visual programming.

   BIAS is capable of general‐purpose programming, but is classified here as an esoteric programming language (esolang) due to its unconventional visual syntax. The language was developed with assistance from Microsoft Copilot.

   BIAS was not intended to be a parody (e.g., INTERCAL), a work of software art (e.g., Piet), or a deliberate obfuscation (e.g., MALBOLGE). BIAS was a low‐stakes project for testing the capabilities of Microsoft Copilot, an AI tool needing no investment of time or money before use, in contrast to locally‐trained large language models or fee‐based services.

track.name: AI as tool for software engineering

title: Modeling the sky in VLT/ESPRESSO spectra
abstract:
Accurate sky subtraction is essential for precise flux calibration in high-resolution spectroscopy. For the ESPRESSO spectrograph at the Very Large Telescope (VLT), the official ESO pipeline provides two sky-subtraction strategies: "pixel-by-pixel" subtraction and sky modeling via the "smoothed" method. While pixel-by-pixel subtraction affects the final signal-to-noise ratio in particular for faint targets, the smoothed method leads to a systematic underestimation of the observed flux. This "zero-level problem" manifests as a clear negative offset in saturated absorption regions of quasar spectra, driven by flux error distributions and their subsequent propagation during exposure combination.
In this poster, I will present an alternative approach: the running median method. By constructing a robust sky continuum model, this method is designed to overcome the limitations of both official sky-subtraction strategies. Applying this technique to a sample of 23 high-redshift, ultra-high-resolution quasar spectra, I will evaluate its accuracy, performance, and limitations. From this analysis, I will draw general conclusions to inform the development of future data reduction pipelines for high-resolution spectrographs at the ELTs.

track.name: Topical Computing, Software and Algorithms

title: The real-time visibility reception pipeline for the SKA observatory
abstract:
This talk presents the visibility reception pipeline, the distributed component in charge of continuously receiving the stream of correlated visibility data produced by the SKA Low and SKA Mid telescopes, and multiplexing it for different purposes, including storage, display and real-time calibration. With future data rates in the hundreds of GB/s, the pipeline sits at the front of the data flow of the Science Data Processor, and therefore it has been one of the key pieces of software running in the observatory since construction began.

The talk includes a description of the context and architecture of the pipeline, the requirements it needs to meet, the challenges it still needs to tackle, as well as delving into the many different technologies used across its internal components.

track.name: Building and operating science platforms and workflows in the Petabyte Era

title: Quantum Annealing for Gamma-Ray Source Detection and Localization with AGILE Data
abstract:
The detection and localization of gamma-ray sources is a complex optimization problem, requiring the estimation of parameters such as the source flux, background, position, and detection significance. AGILE is an Italian Space Agency mission whose Gamma-Ray Imaging Detector (GRID) surveyed the sky in the 30 MeV-50 GeV band and produced photon count maps. Detecting gamma-ray sources in this data can be challenging because of low photon counts, which require specific methods to separate the source from the diffuse background. For this reason, the classical approach to detect and localize gamma-ray sources is the Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE). This fitting problem can be seen as an optimization over the model parameters, making it a candidate for quantum annealing, a computational paradigm that solves optimization problems by encoding them into the ground state of an Ising Hamiltonian. This technique does so through a slow, controlled process that evolves into the minimum-energy configuration, which then encodes the solution to the optimization problem, representing a promising approach in the current Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum era. In this work, we reformulate the standard likelihood analysis of AGILE-GRID data as a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) problem, making the cost function quadratic and expressing the model parameters in binary form, as required by a quantum annealer.
