This approach could speed up the analysis of complex data, where the classical MLE fit becomes slow or may fail to converge.
We solve this task with simulated quantum annealing and benchmark it against the classical pipeline implemented in AGILEpy, the official analysis library for the AGILE mission, on 200 simulated observations at extragalactic latitude. Both the classical and quantum approaches recover the source flux accurately, with a systematic error of +2.8% for the former and -0.3% for the latter. For the isotropic background, the mean raw residuals are -0.87 (QUBO) and -0.58 (classical). We also found that the QUBO identifies the correct position among the 81 candidate positions on a grid with of 0.5° resolution in 90% of the maps. These results show that the quantum approach achieves accuracy close to that of the classical pipeline, a promising result for applying quantum annealing to gamma-ray source detection and localization. As a next step, we plan to test the method on real quantum annealing hardware.

track.name: AI as tool for scientific discovery

title: Free your team's knowledge with Cambium - a static site generator for scientific documentation
abstract:
Communication remains the largest barrier to collaboration in science. Astronomy as a field has an enormous wealth of information, compute power, and human drive, but often lacks the ability to connect these together in an efficient way. Typical efforts to coordinate technical and logistical information within and across scientific teams are wildly disparate, require significant overhead, or force scientists to conform to structures not relevant to their needs. 
 
We present Cambium, a static site generator intended to disperse information with as little effort as possible. Cambium works alongside tools familiar to the astronomy community: install with Python, write in Markdown, collaborate with Git, and use any webhost you like. Cambium's focus is to simplify information sharing, by making the transition from individualized notes and scattered datasets to group documentation with annotated data releases as seamless as possible. Cambium can reduce scientific teams' dependence on high-inertia tools such as MediaWiki and Sphinx. Further, Cambium incorporates science-dedicated tooling - with the Astropy toolset Cambium will build in previews for FITS files and data tables out of simple Markdown links. Cambium makes it easy for teams of any size, from small to astronomical, to communicate and collaborate without requiring their members to adopt an alien workflow.

track.name: The art of collaboration in astronomy software development

title: NED's new API
abstract: The NASA/IPAC Extragalactic Database has been serving the astronomy community for over 36 years. We have done a major database refactoring and subsequently the API has gone through a major rewrite. We have also updated the Python Astroquery.ipac.ned package to use the new API. We urge the community to switch to the new API since the old API has been deprecated and could not access any new data ingested since January 2026.

track.name: Topical Computing, Software and Algorithms

title: Radio Signatures of Merger Shocks in Galaxy Groups: Predictions from Cosmological Simulations
abstract: While merger-driven shocks in galaxy clusters are well established cosmic ray accelerators, the recent discovery of extended continuum emission around galaxy groups, called Odd Radio Circles (ORCs), in wide-field radio surveys like EMU (ASKAP) raises the question whether similar processes also operate in less massive environments. Using state-of-the-art numerical models of cosmic ray electron injection and evolution in cosmological context, we investigate the hypothesis that ORCs are radio signatures of merger shocks through high-resolution numerical simulations. We present the first zoom-in simulation of a galaxy group using the on-the-fly spectral cosmic ray solver CRESCENDO within the magnetohydrodynamic SPH code OpenGadget3. In our analysis, we place special emphasis on applying techniques that yield self-consistent mock observational quantities for polarization properties and flux densities, which enables a direct comparison between the model and observed counterparts. This allows to assess the role of diffusive shock acceleration in ORCs and its importance relative to particle injection from supernovae and active galactic nuclei in the energy budget of galaxy groups. The simulation predicts large-scale, diffuse cosmic ray populations in the sub-relativistic regime throughout the circumgalactic medium (CGM), extending beyond the virial radius of ~400 kpc. As increasingly sensitive radio surveys with growing sky coverage produce ever larger data volumes, neural-network-based source classification will be essential for identifying such emission and ultimately in establishing the dominant physical mechanisms shaping the CGM of galaxy groups and even Milky Way-like galaxies.

track.name: AI as tool for scientific discovery

title: Teaching AI in Astronomy
abstract:
Experiences teaching two AI classes for advanced undergraduates will be reported.  In the first example (ASTR320, Theoretical Astrophysics) students were  programming problems using Claude, but the focus was astrophysics.
In the second example (ASTR498I, Special Problems in Astronomy) we take a different approach and let students learn to solve computing problems purely by prompting. This class will be taught in the Fall 2026, and the abstract cannot reflect our experiences yet. At time of presentation we have had two months of experience to report though.
We will also review a number of reported cases of teaching AI in astronomy.

track.name: AI as tool for scientific discovery

title: A Configurable and Reusable Batch-Processing Pipeline for Time-Domain Astronomical Data
abstract:
Time-domain astronomical observations continuously generate large volumes of data that require repeated processing through multiple steps before science-ready data products can be produced and released. As the number of telescopes and observing systems increases, maintaining telescope-specific processing scripts becomes difficult to reuse, monitor, and extend. We present a configurable and reusable batch-processing pipeline designed to support the processing and release of time-domain astronomical data.
The pipeline separates telescope-specific configurations from common processing logic and organizes data reduction into modular steps with clearly defined inputs, outputs, parameters, and quality metrics. Processing states, logs, and data provenance are recorded for each step, allowing users to identify successfully processed data, locate failed tasks, and rerun individual processing stages when necessary. The pipeline is designed for portable deployment in virtualized or standalone computing environments and can be adapted to different telescopes through configuration and processing modules.
Processed science data products are connected to an online data release service that supports data query, visualization, and download. A natural-language query interface based on NL2SQL is also introduced to facilitate data discovery without requiring users to directly construct SQL statements. The current implementation is evaluated using time-domain observational datasets from miniST and the ST prototype, demonstrating the feasibility of a reusable processing and data-service workflow for future multi-telescope applications.

track.name: Building and operating science platforms and workflows in the Petabyte Era

title: Obsolescence Management: Rewrite, Port, or Emulate?
abstract:
The Telescope Control System (TCS) of the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope (CFHT)
is the result of a multi-year directed effort by a team of multiple
specialized software engineers.  Currently we use the 5th generation
known as TCS-V.  The core computer which runs the show still uses VxWorks 5
on 32-bit Sun SPARC hardware from the 90s.  The jump from TCS-IV to TCS-V involved
adding a Linux "PowerPMAC", but even that system is now more than a decade old.
A total rewrite of everything would undoubtedly incur problems we don't
currently have.  It would also cost time on sky for testing, and would
not be expected to improve efficiency or performance.  Yet, it was still essential
that we consider upgrades now that most of the hardware is obsolete.
At the very least, a port to newer computing hardware, and Linux or at
maybe a newer version of VxWorks were considered.  This would be a comparable
turn of the crank as happened between TCS-IV and TCS-V.  Would there be a
more efficient path for an observatory with limited resources and lost
expertise with the old EPICS system?  We considered the third option which
would at least eliminate the hardware worries:  Emulation.  We share some
technical details and status of the SPARC 32 emulator, which has recently
reached a testing phase.

track.name: Topical Computing, Software and Algorithms

title: ATRAN_SDC - Modelling Atmospheric Transmission Spectra for Airborne & Ground-Based Infrared Observations
abstract:
In 1991, Steve Lord released the ATRAN tool for computing atmospheric transmission spectra from the near-infrared to microwave wavelengths. For decades, ATRAN has served as a standard for telluric correction of ground-based and airborne astronomical observations, including several of the infrared instruments that flew aboard the now-decommissioned airborne observatory SOFIA.

At the SOFIA Data Center (SDC, see presentation B. Greiner), revised versions of the original ATRAN code and its spectral line database have been developed, with the permission of the author, incorporating upgrades and fixes matching the specific needs of SOFIA science data. This new model, named ATRAN_SDC, has been used to generate a databank of mid- and far-infrared transmission spectra, with parameters corresponding to the typical atmospheric conditions during SOFIA science operations. These spectra are publicly available on the University of Stuttgart's Data Repository, and are utilised by the data reduction pipeline package "Redux”.

To further improve the access of the global community to these valuable data assets, and adhere to the “FAIR” data principles, the SDC has developed a standalone web application. This interfaces with the ATRAN_SDC code, and allows users to generate fully customised ATRAN_SDC transmission spectra, with a range of relevant parameters, and download them for further analysis and usage on infrared datasets.

This poster will overview the development of the ATRAN_SDC transmission model and transmission spectra, as well as the functionality of the associated web application. It will also explore the integration of the updated spectra into the Redux data reduction pipeline, as part of an enhanced telluric correction for the mid- and far-infrared instruments FORCAST and FIFI-LS.

track.name: Topical Computing, Software and Algorithms

title: How Should We Build the Next Generation of Science Platforms?
abstract:
Science platforms are evolving from data repositories into computing platforms. As data volumes reach tens of petabytes and scientific workflows become increasingly compute-intensive, downloading datasets for local analysis is no longer sustainable. The shift towards bringing code to the data introduces new challenges in scalability, infrastructure management, operational sustainability, and cost. How should we design the next generation of science platforms to meet these demands?
The ESA Datalabs and Archives Cloud Study (EDACS) investigates alternative infrastructure strategies for future science platforms. Rather than assuming a single deployment model, the study evaluates alternative architectural patterns, including expanding existing on-premises infrastructure or adopting a hybrid architecture that extends selected services to cloud-based environments. The assessment considers technical performance, scalability, operational complexity, governance, cost models, sustainability, and opportunities for collaboration with external research infrastructures. ESA Datalabs and selected ESA Science Archives provide representative use cases for this evaluation.
As the study is currently in its early stages, this poster presents the motivation, evaluation framework, and architectural considerations that underpin the assessment. Rather than presenting a completed solution, it aims to engage the ADASS community in discussing deployment strategies, architectural patterns, evaluation criteria, and operational experiences from similar large-scale science platforms. We hope these discussions will help shape a robust decision framework for the next generation of data-intensive science infrastructures.

track.name: Building and operating science platforms and workflows in the Petabyte Era

title: Towards Plug-and-Play Machine Learning in Astronomy
abstract: As in many other disciplines, also in astronomy Machine Learning (ML) is becoming more and more important. Current workflows often force researchers to repeatedly extract and preprocess data in specific formats for using them in their individual ML tools. We present a concept that extends the International Virtual Observatory Alliance (IVOA) vision of interoperability to ML models. Our goal is to enable an easy integration of ML models into existing astronomical tools. By using standardized model representations such as ONNX, our approach enables models to be tested on diverse datasets without significant additional effort. This standardization makes models interchangeable, allows fair comparisons, accelerates iterative development, and simplifies the extension of tools with individual functionalities. Finally, we demonstrate a prototype that integrates various custom-built ML models into the TOPCAT software, showcasing practical applications such as automatic classification or redshift estimation.

track.name: AI as tool for scientific discovery

title: The Keck Observatory Archive Hurtles Towards the 2030s
abstract:
KOA is undergoing an ambitious architectural transformation scheduled for completion in Summer  2027, intended to support accelerating data volumes,  efficient and automated operations, and new user services to meet the needs of modern analysis. Some components have been discussed at earlier ADASS meetings: this presentation will give an holistic view of the architecture, and the benefits of new technologies in developing it.
Automated real-time ingestion of newly acquired data is being extended to include a dedicated data transfer node  to support ingestion of large data volumes  (>100 GB nightly) created by new instruments (LIGER, SCALES, and HISPEC) under development. They that will propel archive holdings from 200 TB to 1 PB, held on-premises at NExScI . At the same time, management of metadata, creation of database schema - including TAP compliant schema -  and creation of the database tables themselves have been fully automated, with AI support.  The creation and management of user accounts for Keck Investigators have also been fully automated.  A new interactive dashboard-based metrics system will report archive content and usage. 
The archive services are under active migration to a query infrastructure based on the Open Source "low-code" Plotly-Dash framework widely used in business, augmented with R-tree based indexing and interfacing with a TAP-server. Altogether, this new query infrastructure is x20 faster than is the case now, and is much more compact and sustainable. It will sit beneath a new landing page.  KOA is participating in an institutional effort to investigate the value of use Agentic AI in new, natural language end-user services.  Thus far, KOA has investigated the use of harness engineering in building AI applications and in synthesizing documentation for users: the harness includes  doom loop detection, a deterministic rule engine and a self-improving verifier training corpus. The harness has proved to take up 80% of the effort in delivering a prototype LLM interface. 
Underpinning the effort just described are migrations to Red Hat Enterprise and PostgreSQL,  support for archive security and access controls, and installations of new hardware. These efforts are coordinated at an institutional level. Given that KOA is operated by a small team, we will summarize the management approach and lessons learned in managing this ambitious enterprise.

track.name: Topical Computing, Software and Algorithms

title: AI assisted observatory management
abstract:
In the past years the field of observatory operations has seen many technical advances which have predominantly been driven by the need for robotisation. Employing the new opportunities provided by AI agents advances this development. The German Centre for Astrophysics (DZA) has launched several projects in this regard. In this contribution we present
(1) Exploitation of libraries of documentation (manufacturer documentation, technical manuals, acceptance protocols for telescopes and receivers, commissioning notations and reports) through a RAG system that incoporates a knowledge graph and an agentic router and that enables queries in a chatbot-like manner which bases information solely on the existing documents. This facilitates efficient access to complex technical information compiled by multiple providers and teams with extended cross-referencing. An example use case is the commissioning of the 14 element array of the MeerKAT-Extension telescopes.
(2) Support of observatory proposal evaluation through a Multi-Agent Review System (MARS). It uses several specialised AI agents that fill different roles in a review process to create structured evaluations that are designed to provide transparent pre-assessments on all aspects of a proposal. Key features include using verifiable evidence as an information base, recording all steps that lead to a quantified assessment or ranking, and using consistent but adaptable scoring frameworks.
We will present the development and current capabilities of these systems as well as the strategies used to verify the results.

track.name: AI as a tool for data discovery and data management

title: RAIL: A Community-driven Library to Estimate Photometric Redshifts for LSST and Beyond
abstract:
The Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) has begun at the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, and is expected to observe around 20 billion galaxies over ten years. The majority of science cases, from cosmology to weak lensing to active galactic nuclei, will need redshifts for these galaxies, but the sheer number of objects will make spectroscopic follow-up for each one impossible. Instead, LSST will provide photometric redshifts (photo-zs). However, photo-zs are not well-represented by point estimates since their probability density functions (PDFs) are typically non-Gaussian, and science cases, such as precision cosmology, will require detailed information about the errors on each estimate. Therefore, LSST will need to publish entire PDFs, rather than a tabular catalogue of photo-z values. Additionally, since there is no consensus on a single photo-z estimation method that clearly provides the best results for every galaxy, multiple PDFs are needed for each source.

The Redshift Assessment Infrastructure Layers (RAIL) library is a software package capable of estimating photo-z PDFs using multiple algorithms, both at scale for use in major pipelines, and on an interactive level for individual exploration. In this talk, we present how the RAIL team created this library to make testing and estimating photo-zs easier not only for LSST but the wider astronomy community.

track.name: The art of collaboration in astronomy software development

title: grex: A Python Pipeline for SOFIA/GREAT Spectral Data Reduction
abstract:
We present grex, a Python pipeline for the reduction
and analysis of spectral line data obtained with the GREAT
instrument aboard the Stratospheric Observatory for Infrared Astronomy (SOFIA).
The pipeline operates directly on FITS files
produced by the GREAT data calibration program (kalibrate),
and is designed to handle the full complexity of large
heterodyne datasets. It covers all stages from
initial data filtering and quality control, to baseline subtraction,
spatial gridding, and spectral cube construction. A central feature is a
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) based baseline correction,
which effectively removes complex spectral baselines even in the
presence of telluric contamination, using a per-mission decomposition
to account for the varying atmospheric conditions across observing flights.
This is particularly important for datasets where a telluric feature
overlaps in velocity with the target line. The pipeline was developed for
and validated on the M51 [CII] SOFIA/GREAT dataset, a large, multi-flight
survey comprising over one million spectra obtained across multiple
observing campaigns, which represents one of the most challenging
reduction problems for the GREAT instrument. The pipeline enables
the reduction of the underexploited [OI] 63 \textmu m dataset and it is built
as a general-purpose tool applicable to any SOFIA/GREAT
data available in the archive.

track.name: Topical Computing, Software and Algorithms

title: A new CARTA controller for scalable deployment across regional centres
abstract:
The Cube Analysis and Rendering Tool for Astronomy (CARTA) is a modern visualisation tool with a client-server architecture, designed to support very large image data sizes.
The current implementation of CARTA allocates a single backend to each user. This works well on the desktop and in simple site deployments, but limits our ability to scale effectively to larger images in a high-performance computing environment, as the backend process can only reside on a single node. Launching a separate backend process per image allows us to distribute computation by allocating processes to multiple nodes, using heuristics based on the image size and available resources. Serving each image from an isolated process also limits the impact of hardware or software failures on individual node.
An extension of this approach would also provide a secure and efficient method for serving files from different locations, such as SKA Regional Centres, allowing users to combine multiple data sources seamlessly in a single frontend environment.
We present an outline of the architecture changes that have been implemented to support this model in a new CARTA controller software package, currently under development.

track.name: Building and operating science platforms and workflows in the Petabyte Era

title: The ALMA spectral line search is now online
abstract:
The ALMA Science Archive (ASA \url{https://almascience.org/aq}) Query interface now allows users to search for lines that have been actually {\it detected} in public ALMA data cubes. To that end, we have run the post-processing softwae ALMA Data Mining Toolkit (ADMIT) on all ALMA data-cubes, once at native resolution and once binned by a factor 16, and have ingested the metadata into the ASA database. Users can now not only search for molecules and transitions, but also for redshifts and source velocities or line intensities. We also offer previews for the detected lines as created by ADMIT.

While we expect this new functionality to be extremely a very useful addition to the ASA, we do note that it comes with a large number of caveats. This is due to the often uncertain or incorrect source redshifts or velocities, as well as partia incompleteness of the information presented in the case that, for example, not all spectral windows in the raw data also were imaged by ALMA. We ask users to proceed with utmost care and use their own scientific judgement.

track.name: Topical Computing, Software and Algorithms

title: VROOM-SBI: Amortized Bayesian QU-Fitting for Survey-Scale Faraday Analysis
abstract:
Faraday rotation along a line of sight is recovered either by Faraday synthesis, which transforms the Stokes Q and U spectra into Faraday depth space, or by QU-fitting, which fits parametric depolarization models directly to Q(λ²) and U(λ²). QU-fitting returns calibrated uncertainties and handles model comparison naturally, but it costs one full Bayesian inference per sightline, typically 10⁴ to 10⁶ forward-model evaluations under a sampler. At survey scale this is prohibitive.

VROOM-SBI removes the sampler. Simulation-based inference never evaluates a likelihood. We draw parameters from the prior, push them through the same forward model QU-fitting already uses (depolarization model, frequency coverage, noise realization), and keep the resulting parameter and spectrum pairs. A neural density estimator learns the mapping from the simulations themselves, so anything the simulator can generate can be inferred, including instrumental effects that are awkward to write into an analytic likelihood.

The specific method is neural posterior estimation. A conditional normalizing flow q(θ | Q, U) is trained on the simulated pairs by maximizing the log-density of the true parameters given their spectra, so the network targets the posterior directly rather than a likelihood or a summary-statistic distance. Training is paid once per depolarization model and frequency setup. Inference on a new sightline is then a single forward pass returning a full posterior in milliseconds. This amortization is the entire source of the 500x speedup over traditional QU-fitting. Our cost scales with the number of models trained, not the number of pixels.

Recovered posteriors agree with Faraday synthesis and classical QU-fitting carried out using RM-Tools, with coverage validated by Tarp testing and simulation based calibration, at roughly 500× lower per-sightline cost. We have released the code on github (https://github.com/skunkworks-ra/vroom-sbi) and trained models via HuggingFace (https://huggingface.co/skunkworks-ra/vroomsbi) currently for L-Band at the VLA.

track.name: AI as tool for scientific discovery

title: A reproducible workflow for multi-frequency radio continuum spectral mapping
abstract: Multi-frequency radio continuum studies often require combining images from different sub-bands, surveys, or telescopes, each with different angular resolutions, pixel grids, image centres, and frequency metadata. These differences can make spectral analysis difficult to reproduce and prone to subtle systematic errors. We present a prototype workflow for generating science-ready spectral maps from heterogeneous radio continuum FITS images. The workflow reads beam and frequency metadata, determines an appropriate common synthesised beam, convolves images to a matched resolution, regrids them to a common user-defined WCS, and packages the matched images into a frequency-tracked cube. The pipeline can then be used to generate spectral maps, uncertainty maps, and goodness-of-fit products, while warning users when large frequency gaps or significant differences in input spatial resolution may affect interpretation. This workflow provides a reproducible and adaptable framework for multi-frequency radio analysis, with the potential to be integrated into broader science platforms such as those being developed for SKA precursor and future SKA science.

track.name: Building and operating science platforms and workflows in the Petabyte Era

title: A robust and scalable deep learning approach for detecting gravitational waves
abstract: We present a hybrid search pipeline for detecting gravitational waves from compact binary coalescences (CBCs): By using the output of matched filtering as an input to a deep learning model, our pipeline is able to detect any CBC composed of neutron stars and stellar mass black holes. We show that our approach is highly complementary to the existing search pipelines, and is resilient to non-gaussian noise artefacts.

track.name: AI as tool for scientific discovery

title: The FIFI-LS Pipeline at the SOFIA Data Center – Preserving the legacy of Far-Infrared Imaging Spectroscopy
abstract:
The SOFIA Data Center (SDC, see presentation B. Greiner) was founded in 2024 at the Institut für Raumfahrtsysteme, Universität Stuttgart, Germany. Its goal is to preserve the entire scientific and technical databank of the former airborne observatory SOFIA, enhance the quality of its contents, and support astronomical research through free and accessible data distribution. Data reprocessing is enabled by an updated version of the data reduction pipeline package "Redux”, incorporating the experience of over a decade of science mission operations and data analysis. The rich scientific legacy of SOFIA’s observations will be consequently made available to the global community in the form of a "Virtual Observatory" (VO) hosted by the University of Stuttgart's Data Repository, adhering to the “FAIR” principles of data assets.

Among the science pipelines being actively maintained at the SDC is that of the imaging spectrometer FIFI-LS, which operated on SOFIA from 2014-2022, delivering a wealth of far-infrared spectral data. Much of this data remains unpublished, and contains astrophysical diagnostics from wavelength ranges that will be out of reach to any observatory for at least the next half-decade. As of mid-2026, work & improvements to the FIFI-LS pipeline are steadily converging, with focus shifting to the reprocessing and subsequent archival of the full dataset on the future VO.

This poster will overview the general functionality of the FIFI-LS pipeline, and present several major data reduction enhancements implemented at the SDC. These include a full flux recalibration, enhanced on-the-fly telluric correction, and the automatic generation of science-ready data products. Additionally, the science data reprocessing & archival strategy will be outlined.

track.name: Topical Computing, Software and Algorithms

title: The Australia Telescope Compact Array "BIGCAT" GPU backend
abstract:
The Australia Telescope Compact Array (ATCA) has been a key Australian radio facility for over 30 years. Its new backend, the Broadband Integrated GPU Correlator for ATCA (BIGCAT), modernises the entire signal-processing chain and doubles the processed bandwidth from 4 to 8 GHz. The upgrade replaces the IF system, digitisers, and correlator, greatly improving spectral flexibility and reliability. BIGCAT uses CSIRO's custom "Jimble" RFSoC digitiser (also deployed on the Parkes/Murriyang telescope) to provide wideband sampling, coarse channelisation, and 100 GbE data transport. The core of the digital signal processing is a GPU cluster that performs geometric corrections, fine channelisation, cross-correlation, and averaging, with software-defined modes enabling high adaptability. The aggregate data rate from the telescopes is ~1.7 Tbps, which must be processed in real time.

BIGCAT has now been in routine operation for six months, and this talk will outline its capabilities and technical advances in light of that experience, along with plans for advanced modes that will support ATCA over the next decade.

track.name: Topical Computing, Software and Algorithms

title: Toward Natural Language Search in the ALMA Science Archive Using LLM Source Descriptions
abstract: The ALMA Science Archive contains over 455,000 FITS images spanning a wide range of astronomical sources but currently lacks natural language search capabilities. We present a proof-of-concept semantic search system operating at the source level: rather than assigning descriptions at the project or observing unit level, we generate one BM25-optimized text description per unique astronomical source by aggregating proposal and publication abstracts from every project that observed that source across the archive. We prompt gpt-4o-mini to extract source type, physical properties, morphological description, and key scientific findings in a form optimized for BM25 retrieval rather than human reading. Of 54,060 unique source names identified in the archive, 10,758 had at least one associated abstract; 8,609 received descriptions and results were indexed into Elasticsearch for free-text retrieval. Comparing BM25 on LLM-extracted descriptions against BM25 on raw abstracts across 20 morphological and astrophysical queries, we find an average overlap of 2.0 out of 5 results, demonstrating that the two retrieval methods are complementary rather than redundant. We further implement an image-text bridge using pre-computed visual similarity scores (Stoehr et al. 2025): for each image without a direct source description, we assess whether its 30 most visually similar images share semantically consistent descriptions and assign a description only when they do, achieving coverage of 44% to 98% of all 455,448 images depending on the consistency threshold applied. This work represents a first step toward natural language search in the ALMA archive. The pipeline is designed for compatibility with locally-hosted models, enabling scaling to the full source catalog.

track.name: AI as a tool for data discovery and data management

title: Results from Improving the Visibility and Citability of Exoplanet Research Software
abstract:
The Astrophysics Source Code Library (ASCL) is a free online registry for software used in astronomy, astrophysics, and planetary science research. As of September 2026, it contains more than 4,100 software entries and is indexed by NASA’s Astrophysics Data System (ADS/SciX) and Clarivate’s Web of Science. NASA’s Exoplanet Modeling and Analysis Center (EMAC), established in 2020, catalogs and hosts resources for exoplanet research, including research software.

In 2025, NASA funded the ASCL to improve the visibility of EMAC software and associated resources through services exoplanet researchers already use, particularly ADS/SciX. The ASCL created new records and augmented existing records for software represented in EMAC, adding links between the two resources and providing citable ASCL identifiers for software that did not already have a recognized citation mechanism. This project also examined whether metadata collected by the ASCL and shared with ADS/SciX might improve the identification and citation of research software. This poster reports this work and its results.

track.name: Topical Computing, Software and Algorithms

title: The Golden Docker Image - A DevOps Approach on How One Environment Can Unfrustrate All.
abstract: Management of software in a secure and modern environment poses many challenges. This includes building and deploying for multiple platforms, virtualization of legacy applications, and package management for complex environments. The Canada France Hawaii Telescope (CFHT) dealt with this dilemma through a containerization of a standard software environment. Labeled the "Golden Image"; this software package provides security, CFHT binary commands, development libraries, network access, common Linux tools, and much more in a secure multi-platform environment for software development for both existing and new projects. The CFHT Golden Docker Image is built through a Continuous Integration and Continuous Development (CI/CD) pipeline through the GitLab application. Two versions are provided: one for development and the second is lightweight for running applications. Other projects pull the Golden Image from a container repository for their development and production needs. The CI/CD pipeline instructions are to be used as a standard template for other projects. This ensures ease of use, use of grouped resource tasks (i.e., compiling, releases), and standardized naming conventions. The Golden Image is pulled as a template by other projects to build their own containers for automatic development. Uniformly, this standard has been a success for standardizing, fast pacing, and providing better security for software development at CFHT. Not only was the implementation of the Golden Success a success, but also how persuasion is a key factor in adopting new technologies and standards.

track.name: The art of collaboration in astronomy software development

title: Towards a unified data infastructure for LOFAR 2.0
abstract:
LOFAR is one of the largest radio interferometers in the world, and the largest in the lower frequencies. In the first decade of its existance, the development has focused on the instrumental capabilities, which over the years have led to many discoveries and sky surveys.

The current development focus is on the migration from the first generation of LOFAR to LOFAR 2.0, which is planned to start observations in 2027. The LOFAR 2.0 development has two focal points. First of all, improving the capabilities of the instrument itself so that more instrumental modes can be used to increase the scientific capabilities. The second focus, which is relevant for this contribution, is making the output data and the end-user facing services around the execution of the observational process more accessible, to support the astronomy community at large making use of our telescope.

In this contribution we will present how the different user-facing services are being built in an integrated way. We do this by applying a uniform look-and-feel for the end user between proposal writing, project management, up to the user ingest of processed data. On top of this, we make sure the different services are also technically integrated, so that a single action flow can be done from within the same interface, and use common services like Federated AAI infrastructure which supports user authorisation across applications.

track.name: Usability, accessibility and security in astronomy software
